notes.meaning: King Zedekiah sent two men to Jeremiah: Pashhur son of Malchijah and the priest Zephaniah. This Pashhur is a different man from the Pashhur who put Jeremiah in the stocks in chapter 20. The book is not in time order. This scene comes years later, when Babylon's army was attacking Jerusalem. Sending such respected men was an honor to Jeremiah, who not long before had felt only shame.

Zedekiah asks Jeremiah to seek the LORD for them. He hopes God will do a miracle, like when He drove away the Assyrian king Sennacherib in Hezekiah's day. But the king only wanted to get out of trouble. He did not want to repent, which means to turn away from sin and back to God. Like Pharaoh with Moses, he wanted the plague gone, not his heart changed.

Jeremiah does not soften God's answer, even though the king had honored him. God says the weapons in their hands will do them no good. The defenders will be pushed back inside the walls, and the enemy will end up in the middle of the city. Calling Himself 'the God of Israel' reminds them that God stays true to His covenant, His promise-bond with Israel, even while He judges the people who broke it.

The worst news is that God Himself will fight against them. 'Outstretched hand and mighty arm' are the words used when God rescued Israel from Egypt. Now that same power is turned against His unfaithful people. Anger is named three ways to show that God's mind is made up.

A terrible sickness will spread inside the walls and kill people and animals alike. The walls might keep out the Babylonians for a while, but they cannot keep out God's judgment. Even the animals dying shows how sin brings a curse on the whole world around us.

Those who live through sickness, war and hunger, even the king and his officials, will be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar. He will show no mercy. The people should not think their king can protect them. This came true when Zedekiah's sons and many nobles were killed and Zedekiah was taken away (2 Kings 25).

God offers the people 'the way of life and the way of death.' These words echo Moses in Deuteronomy 30. But here 'life' does not mean a happy, blessed life. It is a sad choice between two bad things: going into exile, or dying in the city.

Anyone who stays in the city will die by war, hunger or sickness. Anyone who goes out and surrenders to the Babylonians will live. To have your life 'like a spoil of war' means escaping with nothing but your life, like a prize snatched from danger. Surrendering showed a humble heart that accepted God's correction. City leaders called this advice treason, but Jeremiah gave it because God told him to. Matthew Henry adds that no sinner is left without a refuge, though the way of life is humbling.

God has 'set His face' against Jerusalem. That means He has firmly decided to bring disaster on it. The city will be given to the king of Babylon and burned with fire. This came true when Babylon burned Jerusalem (Jeremiah 52:13).

Now a special message goes to the royal house: the king, his family and his officials. Jeremiah does not come to flatter them, even though the king had honored him. He brings honest advice. Even the most powerful people must listen to God's word.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think verses 11-14 were spoken earlier, perhaps in King Jehoiakim's day, and placed here later. Others read verse 11 as a heading, 'Concerning the royal court,' that starts a new section. Keil & Delitzsch argue instead that it belongs to the reply to Zedekiah.

notes.meaning: Calling them 'house of David' reminds them of their godly ancestor and shames them for falling so far from him. Being David's family would not make them safe. They must do justice 'every morning,' meaning promptly and faithfully. They must rescue people who are robbed and crushed by the powerful. If not, God's anger will burn like a fire no one can put out. The older commentators say real change might still lighten their punishment, though not remove it completely.

God speaks to Jerusalem as one who lives in a valley on a rocky height. The city was ringed by hills, with Mount Zion rising up like a rock. The people trusted these natural defenses and boasted, 'Who can come against us?' But God says, 'I am against you.' If God is for us, who can be against us? But if He is against us, who can help us?

God will punish them as their deeds deserve. 'The fruit of your doings' means what their sin naturally grows into. The 'forest' most likely means the city's many cedar houses, packed together like trees. Some think it means the wood brought from Lebanon, or the palace called the House of the Forest of Lebanon. The fire God lights will spread and burn up everything around it.
